matched_examples.note_excerpt: The same recipe without angelica appeared under the name “Cassia-bark powder” (肉桂散) in Excellent Recipes by Su [Shi] and Shen [Kuo] (Su-Shen liangfang 蘇沈良方), a twelfth-century work compiled from eleventh-century material. The recipe was said to treat, among other things, “fits of madness” (發狂). For the importance of foxglove (rehmannia) in the treatment of postpartum bleeding and overly abundant lochia in early imperial medicine, see Lee 2005: 147-48.
matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: strong replenishers of Blood and Qi and treat other illness symptoms as secondary." 73 Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, opening lines of sec. 92, "Postpartum" 產後, in juan 5 (Danxi yiji: 304). "Dispersing the surface" referred to induced sweating, a therapy designed to expel excessive Heat. Like many "Danxi" pronouncements, this one was assembled in the fifteenth century from fragments that had also appeared in the Jingui gouxuan 金匱鉤玄 (late 14th century) and its likely predecessor, a manuscript that was published in 1475 under the title Danxi michuan fangjue 丹溪密傳方訣. See Jingui gouxuan, juan 1, "Shui zhong" 水腫 (Danxi yiji: 99; this passage does not appear in the SKQS ed.): "after childbirth, one must chiefly use massive replenishing of Blood and Qi" (產後必用大補氣血為主); and 3.11b, "Furen ke" 婦人科, "Fa re wu han" 發熱惡寒 (Danxi yiji: 122): "peonies cannot be given postpartum because their acidity and cooling [properties] destroy vital Qi. Dispersing must not be used [to treat] any postpartum disorder." (產後不可下白芍以其酸寒伐生發之氣故也 產後一切病皆不可發散) The first editor of the Danxi xinfa in the 1450s, a man named Yang Xun 楊珣, compiled these passages in his effort to reconstruct Zhu Zhenheng's approach to postpartum problems. See Yang's Danxi xinfa, sec. 102, "Postpartum" 產後, in juan 4 (Liu and Xue 2005: 301). More on the Xinfa and its editions in 5.5. Earlier remarks by Liu Chun 劉純 contained a key difference from the wording of the Danxi xinfa. "Our Danxi xiansheng said that if there are no noxious blockers (如無惡阻) postpartum, one should massively replenish Qi and Blood, and that even if there are other symptoms, they should be treated as offshoots" (Yuji weiji 玉機微義 [1396] 49.58a [LiuYChQ: 436B]. Liu probably copied these instructions from notes or manuscripts, since some of these phrases appeared in Danxi michuan fangjue 丹溪秘傳方訣 (HWHG 5: 210-13). It could be that Yang Xun, who was from Xi'an, read the 1439 edition of Liu's Yuji weiji (which was also made in Xi'an), but his version of Danxi's claims on postpartum disorders was nonetheless cruder than Liu's. The Huizhou editors of the Xinfa simply recopied the resulting sentence from Yang's recension. Zhu's more complex instructions on how a woman who had just given birth should be treated (from Jufang fabui 局方發揮 1.28b; Danxi yiji: 46) were rarely cited. An exception was Lou Ying's Yixue gangmu 醫學綱目 [1396, first printed in 1565] (juan 35, "Chanhou zheng" 產後癥; 1996 [1396]: 811A).

The same recipe was also recommended in Chen Yan's 陳言 Sanyin fang 三因方 (18.9a, first recipe under “Recipes for balancing and replenishing” 調補法; ChenYYQ: 211A); Zhao Zhuquan's Weisheng jia bao chan ke beiyao 衛生家寶產科備要 (1184, juan 7, “postpartum recipes” 產後方, to treat, among other things, “failed Blood assaulting the Heart, Blood dizziness, and mad talking” 敗血衝心, 血運狂語); Yan Yonghe's 嚴用和 Jisheng fang 濟生方 (1253); Jihong's 濟洪 Danliao jiyan fang 澹寮集驗密方 (1283), and most of the major compilations of recipes that were made after the Recipes of the Pharmacy Bureau. Yonglei qinfang 永類鈴方 (1331), Puji fang 普濟方 (first printed in 1406; juan 346, “Postpartum disorders” 產後諸疾門, “Incomplete expulsion of noxious dew postpartum” 產後惡露不盡, “Appended discussion” 附論), and Ui-bang yuch-wi 醫方類聚 (1445); the latter quoted all the previous books as having cited the Black-Spirit powder. For more on the emergence of medical statements through intertextual composition in the Ming dynasty, see Chapter 5, especially 5.1.
